title: Tin cans go to war
body:
Your kitchen trash was now a weapon of war.

19 October 1942. The War Production Board ordered every American town of more than 25,000 people to set up a tin can collection.

The reason was a map. Nearly 90 percent of America's tin had come from Malaya, and Japan's conquest of Southeast Asia cut that supply almost overnight. Tin was suddenly one of the scarcest metals in the country, and every can thrown away was tin the war effort could not replace.

So families got to work. They peeled off the labels, rinsed the cans, cut out the ends, and stepped them flat. Boy Scouts and other youth groups ran the collections, often once a month, and towns were asked to turn in about a ton of prepared cans for every 1,000 people.

Cans had never been salvaged on a large scale before. Now it was a patriotic duty.
photoNote: Harry Cardio, 10, of the Gramercy Boys' Club in New York tears off labels and flattens cans for the tin salvage drive, 1942. International News Photos, public domain.

sources.title: Today in World War II History, Oct. 19, 1942, Sarah Sundin
Moment in Time, Gig Harbor Peninsula Historical Society
